Title: Review of Athens on Trial: The Antidemocratic Tradition in Western Thought
Description: This volume contains Stephen G. Salkever's review of Jennifer Tolbert Roberts's book, *Athens on Trial*, which surveys Western intellectual traditions concerning Athenian democracy and its critics.
VolumeSummary: Stephen G. Salkever's review meticulously analyzes Jennifer Tolbert Roberts's *Athens on Trial*, a book that chronicles the historical evolution of opinions about Athenian democracy. Roberts's work, which is openly sympathetic to democratic Athens, examines criticisms from ancient figures like Thucydides and Plato, alongside later interpretations spanning from ancient Rome to modern scholarship. Salkever highlights Roberts's identification of a class-based opposition in early critiques, yet also acknowledges her nuanced discussion of Athenian democracy's reliance on imperialism and slavery. The review, however, offers a critique of Roberts's philosophical interpretations, suggesting they sometimes oversimplify complex thinkers such as Plato and Machiavelli. Despite these reservations, Salkever ultimately commends *Athens on Trial* as a valuable scholarly compendium for understanding the historical reception of ancient Greek political thought.

Content.Header: Roberts's Thesis and the Ancient Critics of Athenian Democracy
Content.Text:
In the preface, Jennifer Roberts says, "The hostile tradition about Athe-nian democracy, which has its roots in ancient Athens itself, forms the subject matter of this book" (p. xii). Fortunately, in spite of intermittent rhetorical gestures in the direction of Foucauldian genealogy, Roberts's book never seriously purports to uncover the existence of a singular anti-democratic interpretive tradition. Athens on Trial is in fact an uneven but often useful, occasionally amusing, and extensively documented chrono-logical survey of Western opinions about Athenian democracy, pro as well as con, from antiquity to the present. Roberts's sympathy is clearly with democratic Athens and with those who say we today have something to learn from Athenian democracy. A recurrent motif of the book is that critics of Athens fail to acknowledge "the connection between the democratic ethos and the dizzying heights of creative achievement" (p. 312). Nevertheless, she is too good an old-fashioned historian of both ancient institutions and modern scholarship to conceal the hard questions about the extent to which democratic Athens was dependent, both materially and spiritually, on Athe-nian imperialism, chattel slavery, and the subordination of women. Thus she is not always inclined to argue, as many present-day champions of democratic Athens are, that critics of Athenian democracy are driven, whether they know it or not, by class-based opposition to popular rule.

The book is divided into three sections. The first deals with Athenian critics—especially Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle—of Athenian democ-racy. The historical reputation of Athenian democracy has suffered, Roberts believes, because it lacked an ardent and theoretically skilled contemporary advocate. This absence of indigenous theorizing is serious because "the passages in praise of democracy that have survived demonstrate that its admirers differed markedly from its critics in what they saw as the cardinal principles of the system" (p. 35). Aiming to take the place of that missing "native" advocate, Roberts assembles passages from Herodotus, the tragedi-ans and orators, Thucydides' Pericles and Plato's Protagoras to create an image of a regime of enormous vigor in its celebration of humanity in politics and the arts, not a mere anxious safeguard against tyranny: "The Athenian democracy was conceived by its supporters as a dynamic entity energized by the combined commitment and capacity of all its male citi-zens" (p. 47).

While ancient advocates of this "vital, throbbing entity" (p. 84) are hard to find, Greek enemies of Athenian democracy are legion, and they share a hostile and class-based critique, unlike the "Periclean" notion that democ-racy is rule of all the citizens: "To the enemies of democracy, however, it was clear, first, that demo-kratia meant the despotic rule of poor people over rich people, and second, that rich people made better policy than poor people" (p. 49).

Content.Header: Roberts's Interpretation of Philosophers and Historical Surveys
Content.Text:
That such a view existed in Athens is certain. But in attributing it to Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle, Roberts is on shaky ground; there are just too many bits of clear textual counter-evidence, and she is too scrupulous a historian to ignore them. She sustains her thesis against the resistant texts by attributing carelessness or inconsistency to those authors who don't quite fit the antidemocratic mold. Thucydides goes on about the volatility of the demos, but he does give us Pericles; this shows Roberts that "it is not clear that Thucydides indeed devoted a great deal of thought to constitutional questions" (p. 57). Roberts asserts that Plato's major works contain a "thor-ough-going attack on democracy" (p. 76), but notes that Plato also made "forceful attacks on oligarchy" (p.82); she renders Plato's attacks on rich antidemocrats insignificant by asserting that Plato's "writings nonetheless make plain that he was distinctively a Greek aristocrat who shared numer-ous traditional convictions with the bulk of his class" (p. 85). Aristotle is also said to be "squarely within the aristocratic tradition" (p. 87), but Roberts accurately notes that he does praise the collective deliberative capacity of the many (she does not note that Aristotle is even more acidly critical of the rich and well-born than Plato); Roberts explains this conflict away by putting it down to Aristotle's lack of consistency: "He is inconsistent, however, in applying this liberal philosophy to his political system, for he is unable to make up his mind about the civic rights of tradesmen, artisans, and even farmers" (p. 90). Roberts wants us to believe that the Greek philosophers were either committed ideological foes of Athenian democracy, or indeci-sive, inconsistent, and unclear—no consideration is given to the possibility that Plato and company might have a more nuanced position, one that might help clarify our understanding of the Athenian regime and its relation to us.

The second section of the book reviews a variety of accounts of the virtues and vices of democratic Athens that were produced by politicians, philosophers, and historians in ancient Rome, in the city-states of Renais-sance Italy, and in Western Europe and North America during the debates surrounding the revolutions of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. In separate chapters on each of these periods, Roberts surveys what was being said about Athenian democracy and offers some explanations for the views expressed. Her emphasis is on surveying the extraordinarily wide range of views, and such explanations as she offers are sensible and contextual; no attempt is made to carry forward the notion floated in the first section that critics of Athenian democracy are inevitably class enemies of the people.

The final third of the book, dealing with the more self-consciously professional and scholarly works of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, is an excellent and provocative overview. Roberts's narrative of the eventual and still prevailing triumph of the friends of Athenian democracy over its critics identifies two principal sources for that triumph: first, the effort initiated by the German Romantics (Herder, Schiller, Hölderlin, and so on) to find a country of the mind where life was a coherent whole, as an antidote to the fragmentation wrought by modernity; second, the project exemplified by the utilitarian banker-scholar George Grote, friend and ally of the Mills, whose history of Greece established democratic Athens as the true ancestor for the wholly secular liberal democracy he hoped was emerging in En-gland.

Content.Header: Conclusion: Strengths and Weaknesses of Roberts's Work
Content.Text:
Taking these uses of the Greek past as points of departure, Roberts concludes with an encyclopedic discussion of twentieth-century writing on Athenian democracy, highlighting the complex interplay between scholar-ship and political vision.

As her treatment of Greek philosophers indicates, Roberts is not the most sophisticated reader of philosophic texts among present-day ancient historians. Her comments on the discussion of Athens in the work of Ma-chiavelli, Rousseau, and Hegel are similarly inadequate, because she ex-tracts from them only what she can treat as straightforward pro- or anti-Athenian democracy sentiment; how such opinions might appear in the light of the broader philosophic aims and questions of these writers is left entirely aside. Machiavelli is "a man of powerful passions whose emotions were intensely engaged by the political turmoil around him. . . . Not surpris-ingly, classical Athens sparked mixed emotions in Machiavelli" (p. 124). As for the place of Athens in dialectical philosophy of history, "Hegel cannot seem to make up his mind" as to whether Antigone or Creon is at fault (p. 218). The result of this philosophical naïveté is that Roberts treats philoso-phers as though they were either single-minded political partisans or nar-row scholars. Such a treatment not only caricatures philosophy but tends to drain politics and scholarship of their philosophic content, of the access they provide into fundamental questions about human life and thought—politics is not always one-sidedly partisan, and scholarship can be more than pedan-tic Wissenschaft. Nevertheless, Athens on Trial does in the end supply us with considerable material for distinguishing those critical questions about Ath-ens and democracy that are still worth asking from those that are not. The book's shortcomings as an interpretive treatise do not affect its considerable merit as a compendium that will be of interest to everyone concerned with modern appropriations of ancient Greek politics and philosophy.

-Stephen G. Salkever
